catalog_quote: 2. Tonalité. En règle générale, le kete atteste l'inverse du ton du protobantou. On a ainsi : [...] La tonalité du thème nominal dissyllabique a été perturbée étant donné l'amuissement des voyelles finales. Les quatre types tonals du protobantou ont évolué de la manière suivante: *HH > BB ou > B; *BB > HH > H; *HB > BH > B; *BH>HB c'est-à-dire [D]. Le ton de la voyelle finale s'est vraisemblablement reporté sur la syllabe précédente, comme c'est le cas en synchronie. [p. 108] [...] A première vue, le kete semble avoir réduit à trois les quatre types tonals du protobantou. [...] En kete, la tonalité des radicaux verbaux varie selon les dialectes: dans le parler d'Ipila, tous les radicaux portent un morphotonème bas, alors que, dans celui de Musenene, le ton lexical est haut ou bas selon le cas. [...] Dans le dialecte de Katamb, le ton est bas dans les radicaux -CVC-, mais la distinction …

[...] 3. Quantité. La quantité est phonologique en kete. [p. 109]
new_statements.translation: 2. Tonality. As a general rule, Kete shows the inverse of the Proto-Bantu tone. [...] The tone of the final vowel was probably transferred onto the preceding syllable, as is the case synchronically. [...] In Kete the tonality of verb radicals varies by dialect: in the Ipila variety all radicals carry a low morphotoneme, whereas in the Musenene variety the lexical tone is high or low as the case may be. [...] 3. Quantity. Vowel length is phonological in Kete.
new_statements.citation: Kamba Muzenga, J. G. 1994. Réflexes du protobantou en kete. Africana Linguistica 11 (Annales du Musée Royal de l'Afrique Centrale, Sciences humaines 142, Tervuren): 105-126. doi:10.3406/aflin.1994.947
new_statements.locator: § 1-4 Phonologie, '2. Tonalité' and '3. Quantité', pp. 108-109 (PDF pp. 5-6)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (23 pp., Persée iText render, text layer present; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Réflexes du protobantou en kete', author Muzenga Kamba). PDF pp. 5-6 = printed pp. 108-109 carry the section '2. Tonalité' and '3. Quantité' exactly as quoted: p. 108 'En règle générale, le kete atteste l'inverse du ton du protobantou. On a ainsi :'.. 'Le ton de la voyelle finale s'est vraisemblablement reporté sur la syllabe précédente, comme c'est le cas en synchronie.'.. p. 109 'En kete, la tonalité des radicaux verbaux varie selon les dialectes: dans le parler d'Ipila, tous les radicaux portent un morphotonème bas, alors que, dans celui de Musenene, le ton lexical est haut ou bas selon le cas.'.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kete is described as a lexical tone language (high vs low tone, plus a falling tone arising from Proto-Bantu *HB) with phonemic vowel length; the tone of a lost final vowel now sits on the preceding (final) syllable. No word stress or accent is mentioned in any accessible description; the placement of stress, if any, is not stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect differences in tone only: Ipila has levelled all verb radicals to low tone, Katamb keeps the contrast only in derived stems, Musenene keeps a H/L contrast on radicals; noun-theme tone patterns were reshaped by the loss of final vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/morphological tone on noun themes and verb radicals in citation forms (comparative wordlists from the Ipila and Musenene dialects of Kete-sud); nothing about phrase-level prosody or about stress at any level.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe Kete-sud (Guthrie L.21, Glottolog kete1252, ISO kcv): Kamba Muzenga 1994 uses the Ipila and Musenene dialects (with Katamb and Kapang comparisons); De Clercq 1898 describes the speech of the southern Bakete gathered at the Luluabourg mission and notes that the 'Bakete' on the right bank of the Lulua speak noticeably differently. Kete-Nord (Mweka) is only covered by the unopened Mpandanjila-Mwana 1973 mémoire. Glottolog has no separate code for the northern/southern varieties.

sources.note: Section 1-4 'Phonologie' (pp. 105-109, vowels/consonants/2. Tonalité/3. Quantité) treats Kete as a tone language: tones are the inverse of Proto-Bantu, final-vowel tone shifted onto the preceding syllable, a falling tone from *HB, verb-radical tone contrast kept in Musenene but levelled to low in Ipila; vowel length is phonemic. No word 'accent'/stress anywhere in the article (extracted text a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).
